sections.h2: What are the options for selling a house in Wichita Falls?
sections.html:
Three routes are open to a Wichita Falls owner: a brokered listing, a private sale or a cash sale, and repair needs and timing decide between them. A cash sale suits a house with storm damage, an old roof or deferred maintenance, while a listing can suit a house in good order.

Wichita Falls is in southeast Wichita County on the Wichita River, in North Texas near the Oklahoma line. The city is the county seat and the area's main population center, so buyers come from the whole county as well as from the nearby Sheppard Air Force Base community.

  • Sort out the deed, any liens and the mortgage payoff first.
  • Collect permit records for roofs, additions and other work.
  • Compare a listing timeline with a cash closing date before choosing.
  • Ask the title company for a payoff and a list of recorded liens on the property.

sections.h2: How did Wichita Falls grow, and how does it affect houses today?
sections.html:
Wichita Falls was platted in July 1876. The arrival of the first train on September 27, 1882 triggered a lot boom, the town became county seat in November 1883 and was incorporated on July 29, 1889. The city adopted the city manager form of government in 1928.

Oil changed the economy. The Electra field opened in 1911, the Burkburnett fields in 1918, and by 1920 the city had nine refineries and forty-seven factories. Bank deposits rose 400 percent in 1919, and a building boom followed in the early 1920s. Sheppard Field opened in 1941 and became Sheppard Air Force Base in 1948. Refinery activity had practically ceased by 1962, and city leaders then worked to diversify industry.

Population swung with the economy: 1,987 residents in 1890, 43,607 in 1930, 55,200 in 1940 and a peak near 110,100 in 1955, then 101,724 in 1960 and 104,197 in 2000. Industry diversification brought Gates Rubber in 1964 and several other plants through the 1970s, though some later left. A large mall in the southwest corner of the city pulled retail away from downtown.

The lakes tell a similar story. Lake Wichita opened around 1901 and became a recreation center with a streetcar line, a pavilion and a boardwalk, and a municipal auditorium followed in 1927. By 1940 the city counted ninety-two miles of paved streets, seventy-seven manufacturing plants and 741 retail stores. Those figures help explain why so many Wichita Falls neighborhoods date from the 1920s through the 1950s.

That history leaves a mix of housing ages, from 1920s oil boom homes to postwar and later houses. Older homes often need updates to wiring, plumbing and foundations, which is where a repair estimate matters most to a buyer.

sections.h2: How does the 1979 tornado and Wichita Falls weather affect a sale?
sections.html:
The April 10, 1979 tornado swept through the southern part of Wichita Falls, destroyed twenty percent of the dwellings in town and injured more than 3,200 people, according to the Texas State Historical Association. Within three years most damage had been repaired.

That event is one reason local building officials care about permits. Wichita Falls tells homeowners that a roof repair over 500 square feet or a replacement requires a city permit, and that the contractor must obtain it before work starts. The city also says contractors working in the city must be licensed and bonded.

The city's own notice lists resale as a reason to keep permits on file: future buyers may be cautious about major improvements, such as roofing, done without approval. If your roof was replaced after a hail storm, have the permit number and the invoice ready for the buyer. Unpermitted work can also complicate an insurance claim, which the city notes in the same message.

sections.h2: Which Wichita Falls city offices matter when I sell?
sections.html:
Building Inspections, at 1300 Seventh Street, handles permits and inspections, and the city publishes forms, checklists and a fee ordinance on its website. The office phone listed in the city's notice is 940-761-7459.

Water supply is a topic buyers raise in this part of Texas. The primary supply now comes from Lake Arrowhead, built in 1966, after earlier reservoirs including Lake Wichita, Lake Kemp, Lake Diversion and Lake Kickapoo. If a buyer asks about utilities, the city's utility office can answer for a specific address.

The permit notice gives four reasons for a licensed, permitted job: bonded contractors, code compliance, safety inspections and insurance coverage. A homeowner whose roof went in without a permit might find that insurance does not cover damage tied to that work. Seller paperwork that shows a closed permit answers that worry before a buyer raises it, and an invoice from the roofer adds detail.

Any additions, a pool or a roof replacement that happened during your ownership should be matched against permit records. Where a permit was never closed, contact Building Inspections about the steps to resolve it before you list.

sections.h2: How are Wichita County property taxes handled at closing?
sections.html:
The Wichita County Tax Office assesses and collects for eight taxing jurisdictions in the county and disburses almost $120 million a year to them, by its own description. Its site has pages for online payment, penalties and interest, a tax estimator and who the office collects for.

The tax office also follows the Wichita Falls school district's weather closure announcements, so check before a trip in winter. A title company will usually prorate the year's tax between buyer and seller.

sections.h2: What exemptions and legal steps should a Wichita Falls seller know?
sections.html:
The $140,000 school homestead exemption, plus $60,000 more for owners over 65 or disabled, belongs to the owner who qualifies, so they end when you sell. Disabled veterans may qualify for amounts that rise with their disability rating.

The Wichita County Clerk records deeds for property in Wichita Falls. A deed needs a signature and an acknowledgment, and the clerk manual puts the first page at $5.00 with $4.00 for each added page.

If a loan is in default, an auction falls on a month's first Tuesday, following a notice that has been posted and filed for three weeks. Selling before the auction date allows the lender to be paid from the proceeds and can end the foreclosure.

faqs.q: Is a permit required for a roof replacement in Wichita Falls?
faqs.a: Yes, for repairs over 500 square feet or a replacement. The city says the contractor must pull the permit before work begins and must be licensed and bonded. Call Building Inspections if you are unsure.

faqs.q: Who collects property taxes in Wichita County?
faqs.a: The Wichita County Tax Office collects for eight taxing jurisdictions in the county. Its website has pages on penalties and interest, online payment and a tax estimator.

faqs.q: Does the 1979 tornado still matter to Wichita Falls home sellers?
faqs.a: It matters mostly for building history. The tornado destroyed twenty percent of the city's dwellings, and the city now stresses permits on roofing and other major work. Keep permit records for any repairs.

faqs.q: What is the property tax deadline in Wichita County?
faqs.a: The county tax office says taxes are due on or before January 31. State law starts penalty and interest on February 1, and the lien for each year attaches on January 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Wichita Falls house with unpermitted work?
faqs.a: Yes, but a buyer or lender may ask about it. The city notes that missing permits can make future buyers cautious. Ask Building Inspections how to close an old permit before you list.
